headline: Vermont groups push to close voting-access gaps before November election
dek: A state task force and community partners are focusing on disability access, nursing-home voting, homelessness, survivor safety and ballots for incarcerated Vermonters.
body: Vermont officials and voting-rights advocates are working to remove barriers that can keep eligible residents from participating in the November general election. The effort is broader than making a polling place physically accessible: it includes clearer information, transportation, privacy and assistance for people in nursing homes, people without fixed housing, survivors of domestic or sexual violence and people in state custody. [VTDigger reported](https://vtdigger.org/2026/10/04/vermont-officials-and-advocates-tackle-voting-accessibility-concerns-ahead-of-november-election/) on the work Oct. 4.

The work is being coordinated through a voting-accessibility task force launched by Secretary of State Sarah Copeland Hanzas in 2025. The task force’s working groups address people with disabilities, people experiencing homelessness, incarcerated Vermonters and survivors of domestic violence. The secretary’s office says the goal is to identify barriers and develop practical ways to help eligible voters use the systems already available to them.

Nursing homes are a particularly immediate focus. A September guide from the Vermont Health Care Association, developed with input from Vermont Legal Aid’s long-term-care ombudsman, explains how facilities can protect residents’ voting rights while avoiding pressure or interference. The guide says residents may register with assistance if they want it, receive mail ballots, vote in person or use Vermont’s accessible voting equipment. It also tells facilities to document a resident’s permission when staff help with registration or voting. The [association’s guidance](https://www.vhca.net/wp-content/uploads/sites/172/2026/09/Overview-NH-Voting-Rights-Final-2026-1.pdf) says a resident’s choice—not a staff member’s judgment about disability or cognition—should control unless a court has ruled the person legally incompetent.

That guidance followed a July memo from the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. CMS said the memo did not create new regulations, but reminded nursing facilities that residents retain the right to vote and to decline participation. Facilities cannot coerce, discriminate against or improperly influence residents, and people who need help should be able to choose an assistant when state law permits. CMS also encouraged facilities to coordinate with election officials and, where authorized, use bipartisan election workers to reduce the risk of undue influence. The [CMS memo](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/qssam-26-04-nh-original-release-2026-07-20.pdf) described those reminders as enforcement of existing residents’ rights.

For Vermonters with disabilities, the state already offers an accessible voting system at every polling place. The tablet-based system can mark selections on the same paper ballot used by other voters and is intended to let people vote privately and independently. The Secretary of State’s [accessibility page](https://sos.vermont.gov/elections/voters/accessible-voting) also says voters may request help from an election official, bring a person of their choice into the booth, ask for a ballot to be brought to their car or request a replacement ballot if they make a mistake.

The remaining challenge is that statewide tools do not erase local barriers. VTDigger reported that Vermont ranks poorly on disability voting access in an analysis of Census data, and advocates identified gaps in accessible voter information, transportation and the accessibility of some municipal and school-election buildings. Copeland Hanzas told the publication that smaller communities may not have the money to add ramps or elevators or to move an election to another site. Those limitations can matter most in local elections, where a town meeting or school vote may be held in a building that was not designed for every resident who has a right to participate.

The task force is also trying to make voting safer and more practical for people whose circumstances can make a public voter record risky. A voter guide developed with the Vermont Network Against Domestic and Sexual Violence addresses confidentiality and housing concerns for survivors. The secretary’s office is working with the Department of Corrections to forward mail ballots to incarcerated Vermonters and plans to send a voter guide to households statewide. People without a fixed address can register using a shelter or another location where they live, according to the Secretary of State’s [voting-rights information](https://sos.vermont.gov/elections/voters/vermont-voting-rights).

The policy questions are not all settled. Copeland Hanzas told VTDigger she would like to pilot a secure electronic voting option for some municipal elections, but that would require legislative action and a change in state law. In the meantime, the state is emphasizing the options available now: accessible equipment, mail voting, local-clerk assistance and support chosen by the voter. Vermonters who encounter a problem can contact their town or city clerk, the Secretary of State’s Elections Division or the Attorney General’s Office. The practical test before November will be whether those pathways are easy to find and usable in every community, not simply whether they exist on paper.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Vermont voting-access efforts focus on disability and nursing-home barriers
seoDescription: Vermont officials and advocates are working to improve voting access for disabled, unhoused, nursing-home and other residents before November.
